title: Stress and strain
prior_knowledge_summary: Extension is final length minus original length.
Force-extension graphs describe an object’s response and their initial gradient can represent spring constant.
new_learning: Define and calculate tensile strain as a dimensionless ratio.
Distinguish object-level force and extension from size-normalised material quantities.
not_yet_taught: Young modulus as stress divided by strain

visual_planning.reason: Six distinct visuals support the size-comparison puzzle, area selection, formula meaning, circular-area procedure, strain ratio and synthesis.
visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.title: Why can the same force be gentle or severe?
content: Pull a thick cord and a thin wire with the same force. The force is equal, but it is spread across very different cross-sectional areas. The thin wire experiences a more concentrated loading.
Now stretch two samples by the same 1 mm. If one began at 20 mm and the other at 2 m, the same extension is not the same relative change. We need two size-normalised quantities.

figure.brief: Split sketch: same force on thick and thin samples, then same extension on short and long samples.
figure.alt_text: Equal forces act on different areas and equal extensions act on different original lengths.

blocks.title: Stress measures force concentration
content: Stress is force per unit cross-sectional area. Use the cross-sectional area perpendicular to the tensile force.
F is force in newtons, A is cross-sectional area in square metres, and stress σ has unit N m⁻², called the pascal, Pa.
For the same force, halving area doubles stress. Stress is not the force itself.

figure.brief: Draw a wire cut perpendicular to its length with the circular end face coloured and labelled A; show tensile arrows along the wire.
figure.alt_text: A wire’s cross-sectional end area is highlighted perpendicular to the tensile force.

blocks.title: Stress in a circular wire
content: A wire of diameter 0.80 mm carries 50 N. Convert diameter: d = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ m, so radius r = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ m.
Check: a small area under a moderate force should give a large stress.

figure.brief: Annotated calculation ladder: mm to m, diameter to radius, circular area, then stress, with units on every line.
figure.alt_text: A worked layout calculates cross-sectional area and stress for a circular wire.

blocks.title: Strain measures fractional change
blocks.accepted_definition: extension divided by the original length
content: Strain is extension divided by the original length. ΔL is extension and L is original length. Both must use the same length unit.
Because strain divides one length by another, the units cancel. Strain is dimensionless. It may be written as a decimal or percentage, but keep the form requested.

figure.brief: Before-and-after sample with original length L and extension bracket ΔL, then the ratio ΔL/L in a unit-cancellation bubble.
figure.alt_text: A sample’s extension is divided by original length to form dimensionless strain.

blocks.title: Same extension, different strain
content: Sample P is 0.50 m long and extends 1.0 mm. εP = 0.0010/0.50 = 0.0020.
Sample Q is 2.0 m long and also extends 1.0 mm. εQ = 0.0010/2.0 = 0.00050.
P has four times the strain because the same extension is a larger fraction of its original length. This is why extension alone cannot compare differently sized samples.

figure.brief: Side-by-side short and long samples with equal 1.0 mm extension brackets and different fraction bars.
figure.alt_text: Equal extensions produce different strains for samples with different original lengths.

blocks.title: Do not mix the normalising quantities
content: Stress divides force by cross-sectional area. Strain divides extension by original length. Swapping area and length creates quantities with no intended physical meaning.
A second trap is using final length in the strain denominator. The controlled definition requires original length.

figure.brief: Two-column comparison card: stress F/A with cross-section sketch, strain ΔL/L with length sketch, plus crossed-out swapped denominators.
figure.alt_text: Stress and strain formulas are compared with their correct geometric quantities.

blocks.title: A reliable two-ratio routine
content: For stress: resolve force and cross-sectional area in SI units, then use σ = F/A. For strain: find extension, use original length, keep units consistent, then use ε = ΔL/L.
Do not divide stress by strain yet. That ratio is Young modulus and belongs to the next lesson.

skills_students_can_now_use: calculate stress from force and cross-sectional area
